claim: Mice use whiskers to detect obstacles and drive rapid responses to avoid collision even at high speeds.
source: Our results support this hypothesis, demonstrating that mice use whiskers to detect obstacles, determine their location, and drive rapid responses to avoid collision even at high speeds.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing obstacle clearance behavior with and without whiskers (Figure 2), and kinematic analysis demonstrating rapid modifications after whisker contact (Figure 3).

claim: Mice cleared obstacles at high rates even for high obstacles.
source: All paws cleared the obstacle at high rates even for high obstacles.
evidence: Figure 1D shows obstacle clearance success rate as a function of obstacle height for each paw, demonstrating high success rates across obstacle heights.

claim: Mice maintained high running speeds even as they stepped over the obstacle.
source: Notably, mice maintained high running speeds even as they stepped over the obstacle (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Video 2).
evidence: Figure 1E shows average running velocity as a function of position relative to the obstacle, demonstrating maintained high speeds.

claim: Mice ran approximately 5 times faster than mice in Asante et al., 2010 and approximately 30% faster than cats in Drew et al., 1996.
source: Mice in our paradigm ran ~5 times faster than the mice in Asante et al., 2010 and ~30% faster than the cats in Drew et al., 1996.
evidence: Comparison with published literature on obstacle avoidance speeds in other studies.

claim: Mice ran mostly in a trot pattern, wherein diagonal pairs of limbs move together but are antiphase with the opposite pair.
source: Kinematic analysis revealed that mice ran mostly in a trot pattern, wherein diagonal pairs of limbs move together but are antiphase with the opposite pair (Figure 1H; Bellardita and Kiehn, 2015; Machado et al., 2015).
evidence: Figure 1H shows Hildebrand plots revealing trot gaits during normal locomotion and obstacle clearance. Also supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The trot pattern was usually maintained during obstacle clearance, such that paws cleared the obstacle sequentially: leading forelimb, trailing forelimb, leading hindlimb, and trailing hindlimb.
source: Consistent with previous studies of obstacle avoidance in freely moving rodents (Aoki et al., 2012; Sato et al., 2012; Setogawa et al., 2015), this pattern was usually maintained during obstacle clearance, such that paws cleared the obstacle sequentially: leading forelimb (LF), trailing forelimb (TF), leading hindlimb (LH), and trailing hindlimb (TH) (Figure 1F–H).
evidence: Figure 1F-H shows sequential paw clearance patterns. Also supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mice made large adjustments to the trajectories of all paws as they cleared the obstacle, lifting them 2-3 times higher than control steps.
source: Mice made large adjustments to the trajectories of all paws as they cleared the obstacle, lifting them 2–3 times higher (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D; p<10−10 for all paws)
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 1D shows step height comparisons between obstacle and control steps with statistical significance.

claim: Mice extended their paws further during obstacle clearance compared to control steps.
source: and extending them further (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E; LF, p<0.05; TF, p<0.001; LH, p<0.01; TH, p<0.01) than control steps
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 1E shows step length comparisons with statistical significance for each paw.

claim: There is a clear relationship between obstacle height and paw height, with mice stepping higher to clear higher obstacles.
source: Furthermore, we found a clear relationship between obstacle height and paw height, with mice stepping higher to clear higher obstacles (Figure 1G,I,J; Asante et al., 2010; Aoki et al., 2012; Sato et al., 2012).
evidence: Figure 1G, I, J show correlations between obstacle height and paw height. Also supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Head-fixed mice perform a rapid sensorimotor transformation in which information about the location and height of an obstacle is transformed into graded adjustments of the kinematics of all four limbs to avoid collision.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that head-fixed mice perform a rapid sensorimotor transformation in which information about the location and height of an obstacle is transformed into graded adjustments of the kinematics of all four limbs to avoid collision.
evidence: Inference based on the kinematic data showing height and position adjustments correlated with obstacle properties.

claim: Without visual input, mice maintained obstacle clearance performance without slowing down.
source: Remarkably, without visual input mice maintained this level of performance without slowing down (Figure 2E).
evidence: Figure 2E shows velocity profiles in different sensory conditions, demonstrating maintained speed without vision.

claim: In the absence of visual input, mice cleared the obstacle at similar rates compared to when they had both vision and whiskers.
source: In the absence of visual input mice cleared the obstacle at similar rates (Figure 2B; p=0.19)
evidence: Figure 2B shows success rates across sensory conditions with statistical comparison.

claim: Without vision, mice matched the height of their paws to the height of the obstacle to a similar extent as with vision and whiskers.
source: matched the height of the paws to the height of the obstacle to a similar extent (Figure 2C–D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B; p=0.57 for the leading forepaw)
evidence: Figure 2C-D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B show paw-obstacle correlations across sensory conditions with statistical comparison.

claim: When the obstacle was visible but mice had no whiskers, success rates dropped.
source: When the obstacle was visible but mice had no whiskers, success rates dropped (Figure 2B; p<0.01)
evidence: Figure 2B shows success rates with statistical comparison between conditions.

claim: Whisker trimming abolished the correlation between the height of the leading forepaw and that of the obstacle.
source: Rather than affecting overall step height, whisker trimming abolished the correlation between the height of the leading forepaw and that of the obstacle (Figure 2C–D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B; p<0.001)
evidence: Figure 2C-D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B show loss of paw-obstacle correlation after whisker trimming with statistical significance.

claim: Whiskers, rather than vision, are necessary for estimating obstacle height.
source: suggesting that whiskers – rather than vision – are necessary for estimating obstacle height.
evidence: Inference based on the loss of paw-obstacle height correlation when whiskers are trimmed but not when vision is removed.

claim: The ability to adjust paw height to obstacle height required more than one whisker.
source: The ability to adjust the paw height to the height of the obstacle required more than one whisker (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1D shows performance as whiskers were gradually trimmed.

claim: Mice combine information from multiple whiskers to determine both the height and horizontal position of the obstacle.
source: These results suggest mice combine information from multiple whiskers to determine both the height and horizontal position of the obstacle.
evidence: Inference based on the gradual whisker trimming experiment showing degraded performance with fewer whiskers.

claim: Mice with whiskers but no vision positioned their trailing forepaw more accurately (with less variability) compared to mice with vision only.
source: Interestingly, mice with whiskers but no vision positioned their trailing forepaw more accurately (with less variability) compared to mice with vision only (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C; p<0.05)
evidence: Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C show landing position variability across sensory conditions with statistical comparison.

claim: With whiskers trimmed and lights off, mice were no longer able to successfully clear the obstacles.
source: However, mice were no longer able to successfully clear the obstacles (Figure 2B; p<0.01)
evidence: Figure 2B shows success rates in the condition without whiskers or vision with statistical comparison.

claim: With whiskers trimmed and lights off, mice could not match the height of their paws to the height of the obstacle.
source: or match the height of their paws to the height of the obstacle (Figure 2C–D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: Figure 2C-D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B show lack of paw-obstacle correlation without whiskers or vision.

claim: Whisker somatosensation is sufficient to drive rapid behavioral modifications during obstacle clearance.
source: Overall, these results demonstrate that whisker somatosensation is sufficient to drive rapid behavioral modifications during obstacle clearance.
evidence: Conclusion based on the experimental data showing intact performance with whiskers alone but not with other sensory modalities alone.

claim: At the moment of whisker contact, a paw will intercept the obstacle within approximately 63 ms if no modifications are made.
source: At the moment of whisker contact, a paw will intercept the obstacle within ~63 ms if no modifications are made
evidence: Calculated from kinematic data as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: At whisker contact, the closest paw is only approximately 32 mm away from the obstacle.
source: and the closest paw is only ~32 mm away from the obstacle (pooled across trials with and without vision) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A; Materials and methods).
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 1A shows distance-to-contact measurements at whisker contact.

claim: The state of the body is highly variable across trials at whisker contact.
source: Moreover, the state of the body is highly variable across trials at whisker contact (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 1B shows overlaid frames at whisker contact demonstrating body state variability.

claim: Mice must rapidly integrate whisker sensory input with information about the state of the body to execute appropriate responses.
source: implying that mice must rapidly integrate whisker sensory input with information about the state of the body to execute appropriate responses.
evidence: Logical inference from the rapid timing constraints and body state variability at whisker contact.

claim: Mice use distinct strategies to clear the obstacle: continuing along expected trajectory, shortening the step, or lengthening the step.
source: On some trials, this paw continues along its expected trajectory, whereas on other trials the step is shortened or lengthened relative to control steps. On shortened trials, the paw is placed in front of the obstacle such that the opposite paw can step over first, and on lengthened trials the paw usually (on 74% of trials) clears the obstacle in one large step.
evidence: Kinematic analysis shown in Figure 3A-B and Video 4 demonstrating different behavioral strategies.

claim: Step modifications were initiated within less than 30 ms of whisker contact.
source: Within less than 30 ms of whisker contact the kinematic trajectory of the forepaw changed significantly (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C; Materials and methods).
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 1C shows kinematic divergence from control trajectories with timing analysis.

claim: Both lengthening and shortening strategies emerged with or without vision, as long as whiskers were present.
source: Both strategies emerged with or without vision (as long as whiskers were present; Figure 3G)
evidence: Figure 3G shows behavioral strategies across different sensory conditions.

claim: Models predicted the behavioral strategy (lengthening vs. shortening) with 73.0% accuracy using eight predictors.
source: Consistent with a deterministic decision-making process, models predicted the behavioral strategy with 73.0% accuracy using eight predictors (Figure 3C).
evidence: Figure 3C shows GLM accuracy as features are added to the model.

claim: Artificial neural networks trained with the same predictors had comparable accuracy of 73.1%.
source: Artificial neural networks trained with the same predictors had comparable accuracy of 73.1%, suggesting that the decision underlying this behavior may obey a relatively simple logic.
evidence: Comparison of GLM and neural network model performance on the same task.

claim: Mice were less successful on trials in which their decision violated the predictions of the model.
source: Mice were less successful on trials in which their decision violated the predictions of the model (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E; p<0.001), suggesting that correct decision-making facilitates obstacle clearance.
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 1E shows success rates for correct vs. incorrect model predictions with statistical comparison.

claim: The decision is influenced by both the state of the body and the position of the obstacle.
source: The top features selected by the model suggest that the decision is influenced by both the state of the body and the position of the obstacle (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: Figure 3C-D show the predictive features and their relationships to the decision.

claim: The top two features predicting the decision were obstacle proximity (horizontal position of the obstacle at whisker contact) and horizontal paw position.
source: The top two features were obstacle proximity (the horizontal position of the obstacle at whisker contact; blue) and the horizontal paw position (orange).
evidence: Feature importance analysis from the GLM shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Mice are more likely to lengthen their step when whisker contact occurs early in the swing phase.
source: Mice are more likely to lengthen their step when whisker contact occurs early in the swing phase (when the horizontal paw velocity [purple] is low and the horizontal paw position [orange] is further back)
evidence: Analysis of feature relationships to decision shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Mice are more likely to lengthen their step when they are running faster.
source: and when mice are running faster (yellow).
evidence: Analysis of feature relationships to decision shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Mice are less likely to lengthen their step when the obstacle is high and far away.
source: Furthermore, mice are less likely to lengthen their step when the obstacle is high (magenta) and far away (blue).
evidence: Analysis of feature relationships to decision shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The closer the paw would have landed to the obstacle, the more the step is shortened.
source: A clear pattern emerged: the closer the paw would have landed to the obstacle, the more the step is shortened.
evidence: Analysis shown in Figure 3E-F demonstrating relationship between predicted landing position and actual behavior.

claim: When the paw would have landed very close to or beyond the obstacle, mice tend to extend the paw to clear it in one large step.
source: However, when the paw would have landed very close to or beyond the obstacle, mice tend to extend the paw to clear it in one large step.
evidence: Analysis shown in Figure 3E-F demonstrating relationship between predicted landing position and actual behavior.

claim: The integrity of the decision-making process depends upon the whiskers.
source: The integrity of this decision-making process depends upon the whiskers.
evidence: Comparison of decision-making across sensory conditions shown in Figure 3G-H.

claim: When mice have vision but no whiskers, their paw no longer lands cleanly in front of or beyond the obstacle.
source: When mice have vision but no whiskers their paw no longer lands cleanly in front of or beyond the obstacle. Rather, the bimodal landing position distribution, which is characteristic of the decision-making process, becomes diffuse (Figure 3G).
evidence: Figure 3G shows landing position distributions across sensory conditions.

claim: Models trained on whiskers-only trials were less accurate when evaluated on light-only trials.
source: Furthermore, models trained on whiskers-only trials were less accurate when evaluated on light-only trials, suggesting that the decision-making process is meaningfully altered (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F, p<0.05, 'W' vs. 'W → L' conditions).
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 1F shows model accuracy across different training and testing conditions with statistical comparison.

claim: With vision only, mice no longer lengthen or shorten their step based on where it would have landed if no modifications were made.
source: Consistent with this interpretation, mice no longer lengthen or shorten their step based on where it would have landed if no modifications were made (Figure 3H; the predicted [x axis] and actual landing distance [y axis] are similar, such that the landing position distribution clusters around the unity line).
evidence: Figure 3H shows relationship between predicted and actual landing distances across sensory conditions.

claim: Although mice still make kinematic modifications with vision only, these modifications are less accurate and no longer evince the fast decision process that occurs when whiskers are present.
source: Thus, although mice still make kinematic modifications with vision only, these modifications are less accurate and no longer evince the fast decision process that occurs when whiskers are present.
evidence: Inference based on the diffuse landing distributions and altered model accuracy with vision only.

claim: Whiskers are sufficient for driving a rapid, body-state dependent sensorimotor transformation.
source: Although we cannot rule out the possibility that vision could be utilized in more naturalistic, head-free circumstances, these results demonstrate that whiskers are sufficient for driving a rapid, body-state dependent sensorimotor transformation.
evidence: Conclusion based on intact decision-making with whiskers alone but not with vision alone.

claim: Mice with neither whiskers nor vision fail to make modifications except when their paws collide with the obstacle.
source: Finally, mice with neither whiskers nor vision fail to make modifications except when their paws collide with the obstacle (Figure 3G–H)
evidence: Figure 3G-H shows behavioral strategies in the condition without whiskers or vision.

claim: Models trained on trials with neither whiskers nor vision have reduced accuracy.
source: and models trained on these trials have reduced accuracy (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F, p<0.05)
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 1F shows model accuracy for the condition without whiskers or vision with statistical comparison.

claim: Mice lengthen or shorten their steps to avoid collision with the obstacle, choosing between these strategies by integrating information about their body state with sensory information obtained from the whiskers.
source: Collectively, these results show that mice lengthen or shorten their steps to avoid collision with the obstacle, choosing between these strategies by integrating information about their body state with sensory information obtained from the whiskers.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on the GLM analysis and sensory manipulation experiments.

claim: Barrel cortex lesions had small effects on obstacle clearance the following day that recovered within 4 days.
source: Barrel cortex lesions had small effects on obstacle clearance the following day that recovered within 4 days (Video 5).
evidence: Time course of performance after barrel cortex lesions shown in Figure 4C-K.

claim: In animals with contra- or bilateral barrel cortex lesions, there were no effects the first day post-lesion on basic locomotion, including running velocity, the height of the body above the wheel, and body angle.
source: In animals with contra- or bilateral lesions (n = 8), there were no effects the first day post-lesion on basic locomotion, including running velocity, the height of the body above the wheel, and body angle (Figure 4B).
evidence: Figure 4B shows locomotion parameters before and after barrel cortex lesions.

claim: Obstacle clearance rates decreased slightly the day immediately following contralateral barrel cortex lesions but recovered to baseline levels within 4 days.
source: Obstacle clearance rates decreased slightly the day immediately following contralateral lesions but recovered to baseline levels within 4 days (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: Figure 4C-D shows success rates over time after barrel cortex lesions.

claim: The early effects of barrel cortex lesions appear to be due to decreased paw heights during obstacle clearance, which recovered on the same timescale as success rates.
source: The early effects appear to be due to decreased paw heights during obstacle clearance, which recovered on the same timescale as success rates (Figure 4E–F).
evidence: Figure 4E-F shows paw heights over time after barrel cortex lesions.

claim: Contralateral barrel cortex lesions had no effect on the correlation between leading forepaw and obstacle height.
source: Notably, contralateral barrel cortex lesions had no effect on the correlation between leading forepaw and obstacle height (Figure 4G–H).
evidence: Figure 4G-H shows paw-obstacle correlations over time after barrel cortex lesions.

claim: After barrel cortex lesions, whisker trimming significantly decreased success rates.
source: As with non-lesioned animals (Figure 2), whisker trimming significantly decreased success rates (Figure 4D)
evidence: Figure 4D shows success rates after whisker trimming in lesioned animals with statistical comparison.

claim: After barrel cortex lesions, whisker trimming drove decreases in the height of the leading forepaw as it approached the obstacle.
source: drove decreases in the height of the leading forepaw as it approached the obstacle (Figure 4F)
evidence: Figure 4F shows paw heights after whisker trimming in lesioned animals.

claim: After barrel cortex lesions, whisker trimming abolished the correlation between the paw and obstacle height.
source: and abolished the correlation between the paw and obstacle height (Figure 4H).
evidence: Figure 4H shows paw-obstacle correlations after whisker trimming in lesioned animals.

claim: Barrel cortex is dispensable for the obstacle clearance task.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that barrel cortex is dispensable for this task.
evidence: Conclusion based on minimal and transient effects of barrel cortex lesions on task performance.

claim: Silencing forelimb motor cortex impaired obstacle clearance as well as basic aspects of head-fixed locomotion.
source: Silencing forelimb motor cortex impaired obstacle clearance as well as basic aspects of head-fixed locomotion (Video 6).
evidence: Effects of muscimol injections shown in Figure 5B-E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: After unilateral muscimol injections in M1 rostral forelimb area, mice ran slower, lifted their paws to a lesser extent, and exhibited changes in gait.
source: After unilateral injections of muscimol in the M1 rostral forelimb area (Tennant et al., 2011; Figure 5A) mice ran slower, lifted their paws to a lesser extent, and exhibited changes in gait such that the base of the tail was lower and angled contralateral to the side of the injection (Figure 5B, left, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A; p<0.05 for velocity, body angle, and tail height).
evidence: Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A show locomotion parameters after muscimol injections with statistical comparisons.

claim: After motor cortex silencing, paws contacted the obstacle more frequently across obstacle heights.
source: Paws contacted the obstacle more frequently across obstacle heights (Figure 5C, left, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–C)
evidence: Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B-C show success rates after muscimol injections.

claim: After motor cortex silencing, paws were not lifted high enough during obstacle clearance.
source: both because they were not lifted high enough (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D–E)
evidence: Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D-E show paw heights after muscimol injections.

claim: After motor cortex silencing, paws tended to grab the obstacle.
source: and because they tended to grab the obstacle (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Figure 5—figure supplement 1F shows ventral contact rates after muscimol injections.

claim: After motor cortex silencing, the correlation between the height of the leading forepaw and that of the obstacle decreased significantly.
source: The correlation between the height of the leading forepaw and that of the obstacle also decreased significantly (Figure 5D, left; p<0.01).
evidence: Figure 5D shows paw-obstacle correlations after muscimol injections with statistical comparison.

claim: The effects of motor cortex silencing on paw height were greatest for the contralateral hindlimb.
source: The effects on paw height were greatest for the contralateral hindlimb (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D; p<0.001)
evidence: Figure 5—figure supplement 1D shows paw heights for all paws after muscimol injections with statistical comparison.

claim: Among the forepaws, only the contralateral side had significantly decreased success rates after motor cortex silencing.
source: and among the forepaws only the contralateral side had significantly decreased success rates (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Figure 5—figure supplement 1B shows success rates for individual paws after muscimol injections.

claim: The effects of motor cortex silencing on obstacle clearance persisted even when controlling for changes in baseline locomotion.
source: The effects on obstacle clearance persisted even when controlling for changes in baseline locomotion.
evidence: Analysis of matched trials shown in Figure 5B-E (right columns) demonstrating persistent effects.

claim: In matched trials after motor cortex silencing, locomotion in control and manipulated conditions was indistinguishable at whisker contact.
source: In this subpopulation of trials, locomotion in control and manipulated conditions was indistinguishable at whisker contact (Figure 5B, right; p=0.64, 0.47, and 0.47, for velocity, body angle, and tail height, respectively).
evidence: Figure 5B (right) shows matched locomotion parameters with statistical comparisons.

claim: In matched trials after motor cortex silencing, success rate and paw height deficits remained.
source: Nonetheless, success rate and paw height deficits remained, consistent with a direct contribution of motor cortex to obstacle clearance (Figure 5C,E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–E; success rate: p<0.05; paw height: p<0.05 for ipsilateral forelimb and p<0.01 for other paws).
evidence: Figure 5C, E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B-E show performance in matched trials with statistical comparisons.

claim: A slight reduction in the paw-obstacle height correlation was still seen in matched trials after motor cortex silencing, but this trend was not statistically significant.
source: A slight reduction in the paw-obstacle height correlation was still seen in matched trials, but this trend was not statistically significant (Figure 5D, right; p=0.22).
evidence: Figure 5D (right) shows paw-obstacle correlations in matched trials with statistical comparison.

claim: Unilateral motor cortex lesions affected behavior similarly to muscimol.
source: Unilateral lesions affected behavior similarly to muscimol (Figure 5F–J, Figure 5—figure supplement 1; Video 6).
evidence: Figure 5F-J and Figure 5—figure supplement 1 show effects of motor cortex lesions compared to muscimol.

claim: Motor cortex lesions caused deficits in success rates, paw heights, and paw height correlations in addition to deficits in baseline locomotion.
source: There were deficits in success rates, paw heights, and paw height correlations in addition to deficits in baseline locomotion (Figure 5G–J, left, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Figure 5G-J (left) and Figure 5—figure supplement 1 show various performance measures after motor cortex lesions.

claim: The effects of motor cortex lesions on obstacle clearance remained in subsets of pre- and post-lesion trials matched for characteristics of baseline locomotion.
source: The effects on obstacle clearance remained in subsets of pre- and post-lesion trials matched for characteristics of baseline locomotion (Figure 5G–I, right, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Figure 5G-I (right) and Figure 5—figure supplement 1 show performance in matched trials after motor cortex lesions.

claim: Performance largely recovered over a week after motor cortex lesions.
source: Notably, performance largely recovered over a week (Figure 5K).
evidence: Figure 5K shows time course of performance recovery after motor cortex lesions.

claim: After motor cortex lesions, the forepaw in swing at whisker contact was still lengthened or shortened to avoid collision with the obstacle.
source: After motor cortex lesions, the forepaw in swing at whisker contact was still lengthened or shortened to avoid collision with the obstacle (Figure 6A)
evidence: Figure 6A shows kinematic strategies before and after motor cortex lesions.

claim: After motor cortex lesions, the body state and obstacle position remained important determinants of the chosen strategy.
source: and the body state and obstacle position remained important determinants of the chosen strategy: models trained on pre- and post-lesion sessions were comparably accurate in predicting behavior (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A; p=0.06)
evidence: Figure 6—figure supplement 1A shows model accuracy before and after motor cortex lesions with statistical comparison.

claim: After motor cortex lesions, mice were still more likely to lengthen steps if their paw would have landed closer to the obstacle.
source: mice were still more likely to lengthen steps if their paw would have landed closer to the obstacle (Figure 6B)
evidence: Figure 6B shows landing distance distributions conditioned on predicted landing distance after motor cortex lesions.

claim: After motor cortex lesions, the relationships between obstacle position, body state, and behavioral strategy were similar to pre-lesion.
source: and the relationships between obstacle position, body state, and behavioral strategy were similar (Figure 6C).
evidence: Figure 6C shows probability of step lengthening as a function of predictors before and after motor cortex lesions.

claim: Muscimol injections into motor cortex caused a small decrease in model accuracy (6.1% decrease).
source: We observed the same general pattern of results for muscimol injections into motor cortex, other than a small decrease in model accuracy (6.1% decrease; Figure 6—figure supplement 1C–G; p<0.05).
evidence: Figure 6—figure supplement 1C shows model accuracy after muscimol injections with statistical comparison.

claim: The paw in swing at whisker contact tended to land closer to the obstacle in both muscimol and lesion conditions.
source: The paw in swing at whisker contact tended to land closer to the obstacle in both muscimol and lesion conditions (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,D)
evidence: Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,D show landing distances after motor cortex manipulations.

claim: The effect of paws landing closer to the obstacle after motor cortex manipulations is likely attributable to execution deficits.
source: an effect that is likely attributable to execution deficits similar to those described above (Figure 5).
evidence: Inference based on the execution deficits observed in Figure 5.

claim: After motor cortex manipulations, mice still decide to lengthen or shorten their steps, as evinced by the bimodality of landing position distributions, but are less capable of executing the chosen strategy.
source: It appears that mice still decide to lengthen or shorten their steps, as evinced by the bimodality of landing position distributions (Figure 6A,B), but are less capable of executing the chosen strategy.
evidence: Figure 6A-B show bimodal landing distributions after motor cortex manipulations, suggesting intact decision-making with impaired execution.

claim: Barrel cortex lesions had minimal impact on the decision-making process.
source: Barrel cortex lesions also had minimal impact on the decision-making process.
evidence: Analysis of decision-making after barrel cortex lesions shown in Figure 6D-E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1H-J.

claim: After barrel cortex lesions, the forepaw in swing at whisker contact was still lengthened or shortened to avoid collision with the obstacle.
source: The forepaw in swing at whisker contact was still lengthened or shortened to avoid collision with the obstacle (Figure 6D)
evidence: Figure 6D shows kinematic strategies before and after barrel cortex lesions.

claim: After barrel cortex lesions, models trained on pre- and post-lesion sessions were comparably accurate in predicting behavior.
source: models trained on pre- and post-lesion sessions were comparably accurate in predicting behavior (Figure 6—figure supplement 1H; p=0.67)
evidence: Figure 6—figure supplement 1H shows model accuracy before and after barrel cortex lesions with statistical comparison.

claim: After barrel cortex lesions, mice were still more likely to lengthen steps if their paw would have landed closer to the obstacle.
source: mice were still more likely to lengthen steps if their paw would have landed closer to the obstacle (Figure 6E)
evidence: Figure 6E shows landing distance distributions conditioned on predicted landing distance after barrel cortex lesions.

claim: After barrel cortex lesions, the relationships between obstacle position, body state, and behavioral strategy were similar to pre-lesion.
source: and the relationships between obstacle position, body state, and behavioral strategy were similar (Figure 6—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: Figure 6—figure supplement 1J shows probability of step lengthening as a function of predictors before and after barrel cortex lesions.

claim: Barrel cortex lesions caused the forepaw in swing at whisker contact to land closer to the obstacle, but this effect mostly recovered after 4 days.
source: Lesions caused the forepaw in swing at whisker contact to land closer to the obstacle (Figure 6—figure supplement 1I), but this effect mostly recovered after 4 days, the same period over which other small performance deficits recovered (Figure 4).
evidence: Figure 6—figure supplement 1I shows landing distances over time after barrel cortex lesions.

claim: After complete whisker trimming following barrel cortex lesions, the landing position of the paw was not modified to avoid contact with the obstacle.
source: Finally, after complete whisker trimming the landing position of the paw was not modified to avoid contact with the obstacle (Figure 6D)
evidence: Figure 6D shows kinematic strategies after whisker trimming in lesioned animals.

claim: After whisker trimming following barrel cortex lesions, the paw landed much closer to the obstacle.
source: the paw landed much closer to the obstacle (Figure 6—figure supplement 1I)
evidence: Figure 6—figure supplement 1I shows landing distances after whisker trimming in lesioned animals.

claim: After whisker trimming following barrel cortex lesions, the accuracy of the models decreased significantly.
source: and the accuracy of the models decreased significantly (Figure 6—figure supplement 1H; p<0.01).
evidence: Figure 6—figure supplement 1H shows model accuracy after whisker trimming in lesioned animals with statistical comparison.

claim: After barrel cortex lesions and whisker trimming, mice did not learn to use a different sensory modality to guide decision-making.
source: This verifies that mice did not learn to use a different sensory modality to guide decision-making.
evidence: Inference based on the loss of decision-making accuracy after whisker trimming in lesioned animals.

claim: Whisking is important for guiding locomotion in rodents.
source: Whisking is important for guiding locomotion in rodents (Grant et al., 2012; Arkley et al., 2014; Sofroniew et al., 2014; Grant et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Whiskers span the ground where rodents subsequently place their forepaws.
source: Whiskers span the ground where rodents subsequently place their forepaws (Grant et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Whiskers become protracted during high speed locomotion, suggesting they serve as collision detectors.
source: and become protracted during high speed locomotion, suggesting they serve as collision detectors (Arkley et al., 2014; Sofroniew et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature and inference about function.

claim: The only visually guided anticipatory adjustment observed was a reduction in running speed on light-on trials.
source: Although mice had access to visual information several hundred milliseconds prior to whisker contact, the only visually guided anticipatory adjustment we observed was a reduction in running speed on light-on trials.
evidence: Observation from the experimental data comparing light-on and light-off trials.

claim: The strategies for obstacle avoidance adopted by mice in the present task contrast with the precise visually guided adjustments of gait observed in humans and cats.
